I taught in a classroom for children (grades 3-5) with emotional disabilities for four years. I've been bitten, punched, kicked, spit on, and almost stabbed by students. Ask me anything.
I used to teach kids with emotional disabilities. AMA

What was your coolest student like?

Did you have a lot of support from your administration?

My coolest student was a kid that had schizophrenia and synesthesia. If that wasn't enough for the poor kid, his grandfather also murdered his grandmother and then committed suicide. He was a fairly normal kid compared to my other students. The thing that really set him apart was the questions that he would ask. I would be teaching a subject and after I finished the lesson I would ask the classroom if they had any questions. Most of the time there wouldn't be, but every once in a while this kid would raise his hand and ask something like "What does a dead body look like?", or "Do you think my grandpa is in Hell? My dad says he is.". It would take me a couple seconds to wrap my head around what was being asked, before I could even formulate a response of "Come out to the hall with me."

edit: No, I had absolutely no support from the administration. They hated my classroom because of our poor test scores and how often screams of "FUCK YOU!!" would be heard in the hallways outside of my classroom.
For those of us who don't know: What is an 'emotional' disability? And how does it differ from a mental disability?

Basically, kids with emotional disabilities has issues that make it difficult for them to control themselves in a normal classroom environment. They don't necessarily have learning disabilities (although many do and it often compounds their problems) and often have normal or above normal IQs. But, they have conditions that cause them to have emotional outbursts that require a more restrictive environment. Many of my students had issues like oppositional defiant disorder, conduct disorder, severe ADHD, psychopathy, autism, bi-polar, etc.
What is curriculum like in that environment? Do you have to teach anything you normally wouldn't have to at those grade levels or leave certain things out?

I was basically all the exact same curriculum every other classroom had. I just had to adjust how I taught certain kids to meet their IEPs (Individual Education Plan). I also had to make time for a social worker to come in every couple of days to work with certain kids on socialization techniques and talk about their home situations (which were often horrible).

I see! If you wouldn't mind another question, how do you feel about these types of students being removed from ordinary classrooms? Does it help or hinder their socialization skills? I understand they're usually disruptive, but shouldn't it be a goal to reintegrate them with their peers?

I used to have this conversation with other spec. ed. teachers all the time. Our general consensus was that it probably harms the kid's socialization, but at younger ages (<6th grade) it is probably better for everyone. When kids have these kinds of issues when they are young they just don't have the emotional control necessary to be in almost any normal classroom environment. They would be a huge distraction for everyone and harm every other kids' education.

From 6th grade on though, mainstream them. By 6th grade most of the kids with really SERIOUS issues have already filtered out of the system. The ones that are left have usually figured out enough emotional control to handle a classroom without having an outburst. Also, once the hormones hit and they start looking at the opposite sex and lot of social pressure to normalize comes into play. They will try hard to not be "the crazy kid".
